title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 13: the field and the one who knows it
excerpt: An original meaning and contextual explanation of every verse about embodiment, knowledge, nature and the knower.
introHtml:
Arjuna asks about nature, the person, the field, the knower of the field, knowledge and what is to be known. Krishna identifies the body as the field, explains its constituents and the qualities called knowledge, and describes Brahman, nature, the experiencer and liberation. The chapter distinguishes the activities of nature from the self that neither acts nor is stained.

This reader numbers Arjuna’s opening question as 13.1, making this a 35-verse chapter. Editions that omit or leave that question unnumbered begin Krishna’s reply at 13.1; their later verse references are therefore one lower than those used here.

Each Meaning renders the Sanskrit in English. Each Explanation follows the verse’s statements, terms and argument. Named traditional interpretations are distinguished where they differ. [1–3]

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: Keshava, I wish to understand nature and spirit, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and what is to be known.
verses.explanationHtml: The question gathers three pairs without assuming that their members are identical. Nature and spirit concern the conditions of experience and the experiencer; field and knower make that relationship easier to examine; knowledge and its object ask how understanding becomes possible. Arjuna is asking for distinctions that can guide liberation. In this edition his question supplies the opening verse, so Krishna’s first answer follows as 13.2.

verses.meaningHtml: The Lord said: Son of Kunti, this body is called the field. Those who understand these matters call the one who knows it the knower of the field.
verses.explanationHtml: The body is the field, and the conscious self that knows the body is its knower. Bodily sensations, actions and changes belong to what is known. The distinction between the two supplies the chapter’s central terms: kshetra, the field, and kshetrajna, the knower of the field. Krishna will explain their nature and relationship.

verses.meaningHtml: Know me also as the knower in every field, Bharata. Knowledge of the field and its knower is what I consider knowledge.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna declares himself the knower in every body and calls knowledge of field and knower true knowledge. Shankara explains the many knowers as the one Self appearing distinct through bodily limitations. Ramanuja distinguishes individual selves from the Lord, who knows and governs them all. The difference concerns the relation between the individual knower and the divine knower. [3]

verses.meaningHtml: Hear from me briefly what that field is, what it is like, how it changes, what arises from what, and who its knower is and what its powers are.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna announces what he will explain: the field’s nature, its modifications and origins, and the identity and powers of its knower. The account of the field includes physical elements, senses and mental faculties. The account of its knower concerns the conscious principle distinguished from those constituents and changes.

verses.meaningHtml: Sages have sung of this in many ways, separately in various sacred hymns, and in firmly reasoned statements concerning Brahman.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that sages have taught the field and its knower through sacred hymns and reasoned statements concerning Brahman. The expression brahma-sutra-pada can denote formulations about Brahman; its identification with the Brahma Sutras is a further interpretive question. The verse invokes both inherited sacred teaching and argument in support of the account that follows.

verses.meaningHtml: The great elements, ego, understanding and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one mind; and the five objects of the senses—
verses.explanationHtml: The field includes the five great elements, ego, understanding, unmanifest nature, ten senses, mind and five sense objects. The ten senses comprise five capacities of perception and five of action. Mind, ego and understanding are included among nature’s constituents alongside the physical elements. They belong to the field that is known, rather than constituting the knower.

verses.meaningHtml: Desire and aversion, pleasure and pain, the bodily aggregate, awareness within it and sustaining resolve: this is the field, briefly described together with its changes.
verses.explanationHtml: Desire, aversion, pleasure and pain are modifications of the field. The bodily aggregate, its conscious functioning and the resolve that sustains it also belong to this description. Krishna thus includes physical and mental life in the field. These changing conditions are distinguished from the knower whose nature the chapter is explaining.

verses.meaningHtml: Humility, freedom from pretence, non-injury, patience, straightforwardness, attendance upon a teacher, purity, steadiness and self-restraint—
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna begins the list he will call knowledge with humility, sincerity, non-injury, patience and straightforwardness. Service to a teacher, purity, steadiness and self-restraint complete this verse’s list. These are disciplines required for knowledge of the self. The passage treats the seeker’s conduct and restraint as part of the preparation for that knowledge.

verses.meaningHtml: Dispassion toward sense objects, freedom from egoism, and repeated consideration of the suffering and limitation involved in birth, death, old age and illness—
verses.explanationHtml: Dispassion means turning away from attachment to sense objects; freedom from egoism means relinquishing the claim of “I.” Repeated contemplation of birth, death, old age and disease recognises the suffering inherent in embodied existence. Krishna includes this recognition among the conditions of knowledge, alongside the disciplines listed before and after it.

verses.meaningHtml: Non-attachment, freedom from possessive clinging to children, spouse, home and the like, and a consistently even mind when desired or undesired events occur—
verses.explanationHtml: The required detachment extends to children, spouse, home and similar attachments. Anabhishvanga denotes freedom from intense clinging to them. Krishna also requires an even mind when either desired or undesired events occur. Together these qualities describe freedom from the family attachments and changes of fortune that otherwise bind the person to embodied life.

verses.meaningHtml: Unswerving devotion to me through undivided yoga, a liking for secluded places, and little delight in crowded social gatherings—
verses.explanationHtml: Unswerving devotion to Krishna is included in the account of knowledge. The devotion is undivided, directed to him without another object. Preference for secluded places and lack of delight in social gatherings accompany it. The verse places devotion, solitude and withdrawal from company among the disciplines of the seeker.

verses.meaningHtml: Constancy in knowledge of the self and insight into the purpose of knowledge of reality: all this is declared to be knowledge. Whatever is otherwise is ignorance.
verses.explanationHtml: The list ends with constancy in knowledge of the self and discernment of the purpose of knowledge of reality. Krishna calls the entire list beginning at 13.8 “knowledge,” and calls what is contrary to it ignorance. These qualities and disciplines are named knowledge because they prepare and sustain the realisation of the self and its liberation.

verses.meaningHtml: I shall describe what is to be known, knowing which one reaches immortality: the beginningless, supreme Brahman, spoken of as neither being nor non-being.
verses.explanationHtml: Knowledge of Brahman is said to bring immortality. Brahman is beginningless and is described as neither sat nor asat, being nor non-being. Those terms cannot define it as they define changing objects. The phrase anadimat param also admits different grammatical readings, concerning whether the passage calls Brahman supreme or describes its relation to Krishna.

verses.meaningHtml: With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and mouths everywhere, with ears everywhere, it stands encompassing everything in the world.
verses.explanationHtml: The reality being described has hands, feet, eyes, heads, mouths and ears everywhere and encompasses the whole world. No single body confines its presence. The many bodily organs through which beings act and perceive are included within this universal description of Brahman, continuing the declaration that Krishna is the knower in every field.

verses.meaningHtml: It appears through the functions of every sense, yet is free of all senses; unattached, it sustains everything; free of the qualities, it nevertheless experiences the qualities.
verses.explanationHtml: Brahman is manifest through every sense’s functions while itself possessing no senses. It sustains all beings without attachment and experiences the qualities while remaining free of them. These paired claims distinguish the supporting, conscious reality from the bodily organs and qualities through which it is encountered. Its presence in nature does not subject it to nature’s limitations.

verses.meaningHtml: It is outside and inside all beings, moving and unmoving. Because of its subtlety it is difficult to know; it is far away and also very near.
verses.explanationHtml: The knowable reality is within and outside all beings and includes both moving and unmoving existence. It is too subtle to be grasped through ordinary perception. It is called far because it is difficult to know, and near because it is present within beings themselves. Its presence is not limited to a particular place.

verses.meaningHtml: Undivided, it stands in beings as though divided. It is to be known as the sustainer of beings, their absorber and their source of coming forth.
verses.explanationHtml: Brahman remains undivided although it appears divided among distinct beings. It sustains them, absorbs them at dissolution and produces them when they arise again. The verse attributes the world’s maintenance, destruction and renewed creation to the same reality. The divisions belong to the beings in which that undivided reality is present.

verses.meaningHtml: It is the light even of lights and is said to be beyond darkness. It is knowledge, what is known and what is reached through knowledge, established in everyone’s heart.
verses.explanationHtml: The reality described is the light of all lights, beyond darkness. Krishna names it as knowledge, the object of knowledge and the goal reached through knowledge. It is established in everyone’s heart. The verse unites the source of illumination, the means of knowing and the ultimate object to be realised in the same reality.

verses.meaningHtml: Thus the field, knowledge and what is to be known have been briefly explained. My devotee, understanding this, becomes fit to attain my state.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna gathers the preceding teaching under field, knowledge and the knowable. The field comprises bodily and mental conditions; knowledge includes the disciplines leading to realisation; the knowable is the reality described as Brahman. His devotee who understands these becomes fit to attain his state. Devotion and knowledge are therefore joined in the stated result.

verses.meaningHtml: Know nature and spirit to be beginningless; know also that changes and the qualities arise from nature.
verses.explanationHtml: Nature and spirit, prakriti and purusha, are both declared beginningless. Nature is the source of modifications and of the qualities that determine embodied experience. Spirit is the conscious experiencer distinguished from those modifications. Their conjunction accounts for embodied existence, and the next verses explain their respective roles in action, experience and rebirth.

verses.meaningHtml: Nature is said to be the cause in the production of effects and instruments; spirit is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain.
verses.explanationHtml: Nature produces the effects and instruments of embodied life, including the body and its faculties. Spirit is the experiencer of pleasure and pain. Krishna assigns these different roles to nature and spirit: one supplies the conditions and operations, while the other experiences what occurs through them. The next verse explains how this experience becomes bondage.

verses.meaningHtml: Spirit, situated in nature, experiences the qualities born of nature. Attachment to those qualities is the cause of its births in favourable and unfavourable wombs.
verses.explanationHtml: Spirit experiences nature’s qualities through its presence in nature. Attachment to those qualities causes birth in good and evil wombs. The verse gives a direct account of rebirth: association and attachment bind the conscious self to successive embodiments, whose conditions differ according to that attachment. Knowledge of spirit and nature is subsequently said to end further birth.

verses.meaningHtml: The supreme spirit in this body is also called the witness, the one who permits, the sustainer, the experiencer, the great Lord and the supreme Self.
verses.explanationHtml: The puruṣa present in the body is called witness, permitter, sustainer, experiencer, great Lord and supreme Self. Shankara explains these titles through the supreme Self. Ramanuja applies them to the individual self, superior to and governing its body, senses and mind. Their readings differ over whom the titles identify. [3]

verses.meaningHtml: Whoever knows spirit and nature together with the qualities in this way is not born again, however that person may be living.
verses.explanationHtml: Knowing spirit, nature and the qualities ends rebirth, whatever the knower’s manner of living. This is the promised result of understanding the distinction just explained. Spirit’s attachment to nature’s qualities causes repeated embodiment; knowledge releases it from that bond. Krishna presents this knowledge as sufficient to prevent another birth.

verses.meaningHtml: Some see the self within themselves through meditation, by the self; others through the yoga of discriminating knowledge, and still others through the yoga of action.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna names three approaches to seeing the self: meditation, discriminating knowledge and the discipline of action. Meditation sees the self inwardly; sankhya-yoga proceeds through knowledge of the distinction between self and nature; karma-yoga proceeds through disciplined action. The verse recognises these as different means through which the self is realised.

verses.meaningHtml: Others, without knowing in these ways, worship after hearing from others. They too pass beyond death, devoted to what they have heard.
verses.explanationHtml: Those unable to know the self through the preceding approaches can worship after hearing the teaching from others. Devotion to what they have heard is also said to carry them beyond death. Hearing and worship therefore receive a place alongside meditation, discriminating knowledge and action as means of release from repeated mortal existence.

verses.meaningHtml: Whatever being comes into existence, moving or unmoving, know that it arises from the conjunction of field and knower of the field, best of the Bharatas.
verses.explanationHtml: Every being, moving or unmoving, arises through the conjunction of field and knower. The field supplies the bodily and mental conditions; the knower is the conscious principle associated with them. Krishna applies the distinction universally, including beings classed as stationary as well as those that move. Their embodiment depends on this conjunction.

verses.meaningHtml: Whoever sees the supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, undying within the dying, truly sees.
verses.explanationHtml: True seeing recognises the supreme Lord equally present in all beings. Their bodies perish, but the Lord abiding in them does not perish. The equality described concerns that undying divine presence within beings whose bodily forms and lives differ. This knowledge leads into the next verse’s account of freedom from injury to the self.

verses.meaningHtml: Seeing the Lord equally established everywhere, one does not injure the self through the self, and thereby reaches the highest goal.
verses.explanationHtml: Seeing the Lord equally present everywhere, the knower no longer injures the self through the self and reaches the highest goal. The self-injury concerns the ignorance through which the self is identified with perishing bodies and bound to mortal existence. Equal vision of the imperishable Lord removes that error and leads to liberation.

verses.meaningHtml: Whoever sees all actions being performed by nature alone, and sees the self as the non-agent, truly sees.
verses.explanationHtml: All action is performed by nature; the self is not an agent. Krishna calls recognition of these two facts true seeing. Bodily activity, sensory functions and mental processes belong to nature. The conscious self that knows them does not perform them. This distinction between nature’s activity and the self’s non-agency explains how knowledge releases the self from bondage.

verses.meaningHtml: When one sees the separate existence of beings resting in the one, and their expansion from that alone, then one attains Brahman.
verses.explanationHtml: The knower sees the separate beings as resting in one reality and expanding from it. Seeing this unity and its manifestation is said to be attainment of Brahman. The verse repeats the account of an undivided reality present among divided beings, now stating the liberating result of knowing their common ground.

verses.meaningHtml: Because it is beginningless and without the qualities, this imperishable supreme Self, though present in the body, neither acts nor is stained, son of Kunti.
verses.explanationHtml: The supreme Self is imperishable because it has no beginning and possesses none of nature’s qualities. Although present in a body, it neither acts nor receives the stain of action. The body’s activity therefore does not change or contaminate the self. Krishna next explains this relation through the comparisons with space and the sun.

verses.meaningHtml: Just as space, present everywhere, is not stained because of its subtlety, so the self, present throughout the body, is not stained.
verses.explanationHtml: Space pervades things without being stained by them; its subtlety allows it to remain unaffected. The self likewise pervades the body without receiving the stain of its activities. The comparison explains how presence throughout the body is compatible with the self’s freedom from the changes and consequences belonging to bodily existence.

verses.meaningHtml: Just as one sun illuminates this entire world, Bharata, so the knower of the field illuminates the whole field.
verses.explanationHtml: One sun illuminates the whole world; one knower illuminates the whole field. The body, senses and mental faculties are known through the conscious self’s presence. The self is thus distinguished from the field it makes manifest, just as the illuminating sun is distinguished from the world that receives its light.

verses.meaningHtml: Those who know, through the eye of knowledge, the distinction between field and knower, and release from the nature of beings, reach the supreme.
verses.explanationHtml: Those who discern the field from its knower and understand liberation from nature reach the supreme. The “eye of knowledge” is the discernment taught throughout the chapter. Its object is both the difference between body and self and release from the conjunction with nature that produces attachment and repeated birth.
